summary: This Wikipedia article gives an overview of Charleston, South Carolina, covering its history from the post-Revolutionary cotton economy and slave trade through the Jenkins Orphanage musicians and the Porgy and Bess connection, along with its medical, educational, transportation, aviation and geographic features. It also summarizes the city's founding in 1670 as Charles Town, its population figures, and its cultural institutions such as the Charles Towne Library Society and the College of Charleston.
one_line: Overview of Charleston, South Carolina's history, economy, medicine, education, transport, geography and population.
key_facts: Charleston lost the status of state capital to Columbia in 1786.
The invention of the cotton gin in 1793 made short-staple cotton profitable and cotton quickly became South Carolina's major export commodity.
Medical University of South Carolina is the state's first school of medicine and the sixth-oldest continually operating school of medicine in the United States.
By 1860, 3,785 free people of color were in Charleston, nearly 18% of the city's black population and 8% of the total population.
The Brown Fellowship Society was established by free people of color in 1790 for mutual aid, initially as a burial society, and continued until 1945.
The Jenkins Orphanage was established in 1891 by the Rev. Daniel J. Jenkins in Charleston.
The Jenkins Orphanage Band played in the inaugural parades of Presidents Theodore Roosevelt and William Taft.
George Gershwin and DuBose Heyward spent the summer of 1934 at Folly Beach outside of Charleston writing the 'folk opera' Porgy and Bess.
Founded in 1670 as Charles Town in honor of King Charles II of England, Charleston adopted its present name in 1783.
The 2010 census population of Charleston was 120,083, and the city was estimated at 134,385 in 2016.
The Charleston metropolitan area was estimated at 761,155 residents in 2016, the third-largest in the state.
Charleston International Airport is the busiest passenger airport in South Carolina (IATA: CHS, ICAO: KCHS).
The College of Charleston is described as the nation's 13th-oldest university.
The American College of the Building Arts is the only college in the country that offers bachelor's degrees in the building arts.
The Avery Normal Institute was established in 1865 by the American Missionary Association as the first free secondary school for Charleston's African American population.
The first theatre building in America was built in 1736 on the site of today's Dock Street Theatre.
The Charles Towne Library Society was established in 1748, and it helped establish the College of Charles Towne in 1770, the oldest college in South Carolina.
According to the Census Bureau, the city has a total area of 127.5 square miles, of which 109.0 square miles is land and 18.5 square miles is water.
